artworks.title: Myrrha and Cinyras
artworks.description: Zanchi's Baroque canvas in the National Museum in Warsaw stages Ovid's darkest incest: Myrrha and her father Cinyras. The Cypriot princess's crime — and the metamorphosis that will birth Adonis from the myrrh-tree — is painted as a night scene of desire and doom.

artworks.title: Myrrha
artworks.description: Rodin's sculpture isolates Myrrha as a body caught between woman and tree — the Ovidian metamorphosis made flesh. The Cypriot princess who asked to vanish from both life and death becomes a study in shame, desire and wooden transformation.

artworks.title: Myrrha and Cinyras
artworks.description: Solis' woodcut for Ovid's Metamorphoses illustrates the Cinyras–Myrrha episode that ends in the myrrh-tree. Sixteenth-century book illustration carries the Cypriot myth into print — the crime, the flight, and the bark that will open for Adonis.

artworks.title: The Birth of Adonis
artworks.description: Monsiau's neoclassical scene shows Adonis born from Myrrha already half tree — midwives and deities receiving the child from the bark. Ovid's metamorphosis becomes a birth tableau: the princess of Cyprus as living wood and mother in one body.

artworks.title: Birth of Adonis
artworks.description: Montagna's engraving in the National Gallery of Art shows the infant Adonis delivered from Myrrha's transformed trunk. Early Renaissance printmaking fixes the Cypriot princess as the tree that both punishes and preserves her — bark as womb.

popCulture.title: Myrrha
popCulture.description: The incestuous princess turned myrrh-tree remains Ovid's darkest metamorphosis — Adonis born from the bark she became.
